en: *Cheng weishi lun zhangzhong shuyao ji*, Volume One, composed by Dharma Master Zhou.
Regarding the Great Master’s inspired natural talent, he recognized that the term "provisional" (*jia*) in the context of consciousness has two meanings. First:
First, it says: "Although his wisdom and sagacity were innate, he nonetheless understood through insight; he did not need to pay homage at sacred sites or extensively seek out the holy teachings.
Second, it says: "The character is erroneous; it should be the character 'shì' (式), which is glossed as 'to employ. I shall now evaluate all these various [points]."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "receiving the *hánzhàng* (函丈)": *Hán* means "to contain. It refers to the Master containing [the student] within the space of one *zhàng* (丈) while directing and instructing him.

It is also said that he "contains" the student within a space of one *zhàng* for the sake of his close attendance. Regarding the phrase "matters involve handling the *gū* (觚)": *Gū* refers to a writing brush (*biān*), and "handling" means to grasp it.

As for "that which is difficult to proclaim despite grasping the original intent": the ten patriarchs established the initial interpretation, whereas the practice of the present day constitutes the derivative; yet, there may also be those who return to the origin.
To establish a distinct principle, he rejects the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Worthies). This is precisely what Fa Shang’s "Light" [commentary] elucidates.

In citing the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, it merely serves to demonstrate that the original treatise has two names. However, regarding the commentary composed by Dharmapāla, which is titled the *Mārgajñatā-śāstra*:

Vasubandhu composed twenty verses along with their prose (*gadya*), and Dharmapāla subsequently provided a separate commentary on them titled the *Mārgajñatā-śāstra*. Thus, its name differs from that of the original treatise.

The principles of the Way should be explained according to their application. As for the statement that "many [explanations] differ," this refers to the fact that within the treatise, the various interpretations do not always coincide with its original title.
However, when adopting the formal title of the root treatise itself, it is simply *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (The Establishment of Cognition-Only);

this is what constitutes the "establishment" (*siddhi*). What is now referred to as "establishment" (*cheng*) is the establishment by the commentators (*śāstrakāra*), and is not the original title of the treatise itself.
*Sāmantrī* and *taddhita* both signify "extensive" (*vistara*). However, while the former consists of eight case-endings (*vibhakti*), the latter refers to eighteen.

Some commentators explain that *sāmantra* is a transliteration of the sound, named after its metaphorical meaning; although its meaning is broad, explaining it as "level" (*sama*) does not hinder its semantic function.
Here, in order to distinguish it from the eighteen cases, we shall refer only to the eighth case among the eight.
This is what is revered. Now, following the Sanskrit manuscript, there are three characters: *sa-ta-da*. These three form a single sound, resulting in the word *śada*.
Both are from the Sanskrit manuscript; this meaning is difficult to understand and the text is somewhat prolix.

Regarding the division into one, two, and three parts, where there are both provisional (*prajñapti*) and real (*dravya*) explanations within them, these will be discussed separately at the end of the commentary. There are two masters who state that there is a provisional sense, yet they do not go beyond [this].

Regarding their names, as both are currently real, Dignāga’s commentary states: "The reason and the example establish the thesis. In the aforementioned *Nyāyamukha*, each [section] causes one to realize the wisdom of the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
As for the phrase "named after that which is predominantly consciousness-only," the wisdom of the principle is the very nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of *vijñapti-mātra*.
"Yoga" has the meaning of "correspondence" (*saṃyoga*), specifically the correspondence between teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. This constitutes the composition of the treatise.

At this time, not everyone has already attained the corresponding realization; because one wishes for them to realize this correspondence at a later time, it is said that the name is designated based on what is yet to come.
This case is also like this, as [the goal] has not yet been attained. Since it is stated that the teaching and principle are universally applicable, the practice and the fruit are also included.
In order to refute the attachment of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to the reality of all phenomena, this treatise on provisional designation (*prajñapti*) was composed.

The distinction regarding the "pure" refers to non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*); this also belongs to the section explaining the stages (*bhūmi*). Otherwise, non-abiding nirvāṇa would not follow from the fruit [of the path].

Furthermore, regarding the "provisional analytical cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) in the Two Vehicles, one should provide the following questions and answers (*yathāyogam*)... [etc.]

Furthermore, that [stage] takes what is subsequently attained as its object, whereas the Bodhisattva does not; thus there is a difference. Now, to clarify what is venerated, the intention is to take the "fulfillment" (*paripūrṇa*);
"part" (*bhāga*) also refers to a "stage" (*avasthā*). The intention is to reveal that the nature of *nirvāṇa* is intrinsically pure.

Regarding the phrase "they are distinct because they have reached [their goal]," the word "part" used here also refers to a stage. Because intrinsic purity is gradually perfected, it is said they are "distinct. Although there are seven [stages],...

Explanation: Regarding these three commentaries, there are four [versions]. However, according to the fundamental meaning, this is the correct interpretation within the commentary itself, which accords with the intent of the treatise.

Regarding the roots (*indriya*), their bases (*āśraya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*)—within the five [categories]—there is *tāni saṅga*. Here, the sound *ā* is read with an elevated tone (*udātta*). There are eight *āmantraṇī* and five *vibhakti-saṅga*.
The character *saṅga* is the "sorrow" of the character 哀 (āi); it is identical to the character 拽 (yè). In total, combining the general and the specific, there are ninety-six sounds.
As for "those," there are twenty-four [instances] consisting of one, two, many, and eight. There are twenty-four each for the three genders—masculine and so forth—making seventy-two in total.
Furthermore, there are twenty-four [instances] consisting of eight each for the masculine and the others; this is the general [classification].

Regarding *dvipadāna*, it is not the character *kuǒ*. The characters [多*頁] (*tǎng*) and [口*栗] (with the second tone) refer to the preceding [category], which is the general designation for all within the masculine gender.

Because it generally refers to all masculine sounds. If *he-puruṣa* (man) is used, within that general category, the term *puruṣa* is specifically assigned to denote a male. Regarding the abandonment (*tyāga*), it applies to both [genders].

As for the passage found in the treatise itself, it is precisely this that serves as the definitive example; it is also called "perfectly accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*), and thus one attains realization.

Nirvāṇa: Awakening penetrates both types. Regarding "the purity of taking and discarding the nature of illusion and reality": Question: Consciousness relies on false attachment; all such things are termed "illusory" and are to be discarded.

What is the meaning of this? Answer: There are three interpretations. First, regarding the two meanings of "illusion": (1) All that is empty and illusory refers to the *paratantra* (dependent nature). (2) The delusion of illusory appearances refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).
(3) The capacity for conceptualization—the emotional state—is the *paratantra*, while that which is conceptualized is the *parikalpita*. Thus, the latter is the object of the former's illusion.

[The term] "clinging" (*upādāna*) is so named because it arises from that which is grasped. Among the three [natures], the middle and the last are explained together. In Bhāviveka’s system, within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the first two natures are both empty and thus termed "illusory.

Dharmapāla maintains that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is actually like an illusion; however, here it is spoken of as being "defiled" (*sāsrava*). Regarding the explanation of cultivation and nature: "understanding" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths;

"cultivating the two true contemplations" refers to the study of the two types of emptiness contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); and "realizing the one true principle" refers to the realization of the single truth. These two follow accordingly.

It is appropriate. The text is concise yet its meaning is comprehensive; the compassionate author composed this treatise so that people might easily understand it, revealing worldly principles and attaining excellence.
It can be understood by correlating [the stages] with the four aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Some say they may also be correlated with the four realities (*satya*);
this interpretation is somewhat more stable in terms of both text and meaning. Regarding "briefly equalizing three or four," "briefly equalizing" means to extensively reveal equality. Three or four.

The three [categories] correspond to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The four correspond to the two treatises. Furthermore, the two correspond to the two gates of the "conforming reality" (*anuvartana-tattva*).

Furthermore, the four correspond to the four contemplative gates of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth. This single line merely summarizes the ten explanations of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the three—namely, the correct and equal [nature].
To summarize, these are the indeterminate natures of wrong view and right view. Regarding "disciples who dwell together" and "those who dwell nearby":
although the eightfold precept near-dwelling (*upavāsa*) is not different [in its substance], there is a distinction in how they dwell together; therefore, they are explained separately.

As for "those who practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), this refers to the combined explanation of those of sharp and dull faculties. "Practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) and "practice in accordance with faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) are to be assigned accordingly. Question: Are these two natures not...
The same applies here. How are they unified? If one adopts the third interpretation, it is the "Additional Interpretation" (*ekavyākhyāna*) found in the *Shuyao* commentary.

Regarding the passage from "producing my dharmas" to "is called 'dispelling'": this is based on the perspective of those who are deluded. Although they cling to existence and do not realize [the truth], both [the preceding two interpretations] are capable of dispelling [delusion].
All are explained based upon the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who are the objects of delusion. The first two interpretations focus on the deluded subject.
Regarding the principle: this interpretation holds that what is deluded about is non-existent; Ximing does not permit this, as it is established by citing the treatise.
As for the statement that Great Bodhi and True Liberation together comprise twelve phrases: these also refer to the aforementioned Great Bodhi.

As for the separate establishment of three phrases for ordinary beings and so forth: ordinary beings do not constitute a phrase; the two vehicles and bodhisattvas each form a partial phrase, thus making three. Furthermore:

Ordinary beings, when compared to the two vehicles, do not possess the Great [Vehicle], nor do they possess Bodhi. When compared to Bodhisattvas, they do not possess the Great [Vehicle], nor do they possess Bodhi.
For the two vehicles, when compared to Bodhisattvas, Bodhi is not Great; however, their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) necessarily entails attachment to persons (*pudgalagrāha*).

This commentary addresses an objection raised by the teacher Bhāviveka, who argued that for one side of the interpretation, the attachment to phenomena must necessarily entail attachment to persons. This [text] explains that it is Dharmapāla who makes this statement.

[This is a] doctrinal point. Alternatively, this text may be erroneous; it should state that it is merely the grasping of persons (pudgala-grāha), which necessarily entails the grasping of dharmas (dharma-grāha).

Thus, there would be no contradiction regarding the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*). However, while the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is not called "grasping" (*grāha*), it is called "heavy" (*guru*). If one were to say that wisdom itself is grasping, [then... the seventh... [would follow].

Eighth, there should be wisdom (*prajñā*). If one says that wisdom is predominant, then the five consciousnesses should also be called predominant. Since the arising of all contaminated minds involves grasping at names, wisdom would then be omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
In this context, since the eighth consciousness and others are likewise associated with wisdom, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the definition presents an obstacle and requires further explanation.
To explain it by way of the causes and effects of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: regarding the causes and effects of saṃsāra—

Thus, by means of the two obstacles—the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena—the causes and conditions for returning to cessation arise; the path of the mind becomes fulfilled; and the abandonment of cyclic existence is revealed, giving rise to the state of returning to cessation.

This leads to the intention of the Buddha-ground and accomplishes the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) as the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*). Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the dharma is restricted": [this refers to the fact that]...
It speaks only of the *ālayavijñāna* because it is designated as "coarse and heavy" (*dausthulya*).

If one were to take only the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and that which is produced by them as being coarse and heavy, and thus apply this to the present text, why does the treatise state: "By means of the grasping at self and phenomena, the two obstacles arise together"?
To answer this objection, it says: "However, due to the two graspings, the two obstacles and so forth arise together. If one relies on this interpretation, [the following] is correct...

Regarding the force of the treatise’s argument: to show that what is called an "inferior transformation" is actually "vast," the first four transformations are explained and assigned to the stages (*bhūmi*), where they belong to the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).
By means of these very four, the inferior transformation of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) is shown to be the "vast transformation.

This refers to the arising of correct understanding and so forth, which are comprehensively included within the text of the treatise. Through this, one attains the removal of inferiority; the remaining five transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) follow accordingly.

Dormancy (*middha*) occurs in the preliminary stage (*pūrvabhāga*) of the sixth and seventh grounds; one portion belongs to the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because the first portion of the seventh ground’s contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is attained therein.

As for those who do not take the ten grounds and so forth [as the basis], this patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) belongs exclusively to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), because it is subsumed under the tenth ground, wherein the obstacles of both [afflictions and cognizable objects] are severed simultaneously within the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*). Other grounds do not sever these two obstacles simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that the two obstacles are severed separately in the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).

From the seventh stage up to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), these are assigned to the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*), precisely because there are two types of ultimate realization. For other passages, consult other sources.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "according to the Dharma, penetrating through cultivation and severance," this refers to the textual passage concerning the arising of ordinary beings and sages; it states that there are two destinies, both of which are objects of grasping—that is, *nimitta* (signs/phenomena).

The *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is termed the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) and the "grasped" (*grāhya*). Therefore, regarding the statement that "the attachment of the noble ones (*ārya*) arises accordingly," and concerning the critique of the treatise:

one should say that "the attachment of the noble ones arises accordingly," rather than stating that "those obstacles are abandoned accordingly. Here, the term "that which is grasped" (*gṛhīta*) refers to the *darśana-bhāga* being grasped by the self-witnessing (*svasaṃvitti*).

This is because the remaining seventh consciousness (*manas*) does not exist during the stage of observing the dharmas (*dharmālambana*). One interpretation states: it is based on the point of ultimate exhaustion.
Regarding the proponent [of this view], my statement that "the roots are severed and the branches removed" is based on the analysis of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

It refers to the ultimate state where there are no further words for exhaustion. This is analogous to the case of the *anāgāmin* who has abandoned desire; it follows the same principle as the other fruits.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the abandonment within," this refers to the detailed explanation of attaining the abandonment of hindrances. As for the division into two parts within the text concerning "attaining the abandonment within," this constitutes the preceding cause.

Regarding the section on the fruits (*phala*), the causes are divided into two parts. To briefly distinguish these for the sake of clarifying the fruits, the summary of the attainment of both ordinary beings and sages within the categories is as follows:

namely, the attainment of the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the attainment of the real (*tattva*), as well as the attainment of awakening and the attainment of abandonment, all clearly explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). As for the four [categories] beginning with resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), they were briefly mentioned in the preceding text; one should look there for full details.
First, there is the position that both object and mind exist together. Bhāviveka [holds] that for the twenty syllables, neither object nor mind exists.

According to one teaching of Bhāviveka, although their functions are distinct, their substance is the same; this is the single intention [of his school]. For the Bodhisattvas, there is nothing apart from the mind.

Regarding the ancient Mahāyāna masters such as Buddhadeva and those of the Sautrāntika school who demonstrate the characteristics of correct cause and effect: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise from causes and effects; they possess causes.
There is a fruit. If one considers the relative distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the cause is conditioned while the fruit is unconditioned.

Because these two stages—the agent that accomplishes and the object accomplished, or the agent that realizes and the object realized—are distinct, the action performed does not perish. This applies to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as to both causes and fruits.

It can refute the arguments of others and avoid [their fallacies]; having already escaped the arguments of others, it establishes its own position. By being free from faults and errors, it liberates others.
This is difficult. There are teachers of the Hīnayāna and those who hold the "Seven Severances" and so forth who maintain that there is severance.

For instance, the Ekavyāvahārikas have such verbal expressions as "there is no principle to be expressed," and so on. Since this is the case, there would be nothing to be practiced; if there is nothing to be practiced, what could there be to be realized?

If there is nothing to be realized, then this cause is severed. Because they raise these questions themselves, it is not [correct]. Next, regarding the second [point], they themselves provisionally pose a question.

Answer: Because there is no cognitive evidence for a light touch; and because the "sovereign" (the self) is that which is taught by the Noble Ones as being distinguished by its functional utility—namely, the stream-enterers and others all possess the function of severing [defilements]. Regarding the statement that "all here are spoken of in terms of the sense of predominance":

these three explanations of the self and one explanation of the dharmas do not exhaustively accord with reason. There are five [meanings] for both the self and the dharmas, and four meanings apply to both; the fifth...
It is translated separately by Bodhiruci as *bhagavat*. Regarding the phrase "not so, [as in the case of] 'one who is born,' 'one who lives,' etc.," it should be stated:

"not so, according to 'one who is born,' 'one who lives,' etc. Since there is no original basis for such a comparison, one simply explains the text according to its literal meaning; this does not contradict the underlying principle.

The commentary itself explains that the term "one who is born" (*jāyamāna*) refers to the sense of a class or category, just as when one says "the classes of sentient beings are not one," implying a plurality of types. Thus, it is so.

It is called "sentient being. Question: Since the mind possesses deliberation (*manasikāra*), why is a designation of "self" (*ātman*) not established separately for its function as a support and object-condition?

Answer: First, because it functions for the sake of others, its meaning is not preeminent; therefore, a "self" is not established. Furthermore, [the notion of self] involves strong conceptualization that causes others to give rise to feelings of superiority or inferiority.
What is meant by "its outflow" (*niṣyanda*)? It means having a similar class or resemblance. What is meant by "attaining the aggregates" (*skandha-prāpti*)? That is to say—

The various states (avasthā) do not lose their names; they become the "agent" (kartṛ). That is to say, the various states are the bondage, and the essence (svabhāva) of the state does not lose [its identity].

Because of these states, one can designate them as "aggregates" (skandha); this is the excellence [of the designation]. Regarding the attainment of the "elements" (dhātu): "element" has the sense of essential nature (svabhāva). It is only when the fundamental substance exists that it can arise and thus be attained.

This is precisely what is meant by "attaining the elements" (*dhātu-lābha*), which carries the sense of "cause. "Bases" (*āyatana*) refers to the locus of support; this carries the sense of "condition.
When combined, they constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). If it is read as the character *de* (德), it should be interpreted accordingly. As for the majority view:

because [the embryo] is mostly nurtured and has not yet been fully formed, it is not called a "person" (*puruṣa*). If one speaks of "opening," this is said according to a minor portion. Regarding the term *du-xing-yi-fan* (杜行[壴*頁]梵): this...
There was a layman of learning and knowledge who was skilled in the "double language" (Sanskrit and Chinese). At that time, he also participated in the translation work;

his name was Di Hui. He asked: "Among all the sutras, which one contains the most cited instances of miraculous efficacy in this land? The Tripitaka Master replied: "When testifying by means of this sutra..."

He immediately ordered the translation of the Sanskrit texts of the Tripiṭaka. [The work] previously at Ci'en Monastery had not yet been completed. Du Xian already possessed a Sanskrit manuscript, which was translated that very night.
As it was required for the occasion, it was promptly circulated; more than five hundred copies were distributed on the same day.
When an attempt was made to polish the text, the Emperor did not permit it. Therefore, the text currently transmitted is based on the three hundred [verses] of Yijing’s draft.
Volume. Among the six hundred volumes, that which can sever the first eight [categories] and so forth is the *Duzhu* (杜[壴*頁]) edition. The initial text explains the cause;
as for the phrase "delivering all sentient beings" (*sarvasattva-paritrāṇa*), since "I" (*ātman*) is the totality, it is logically appropriate to mark it at the beginning.

Because it explains the deliverance of beings, and since "sentient beings" (*sattva*) is the broad heading, there is no interruption in the middle; therefore, this name is abbreviated. Furthermore, it also mentions "I," which is why it exists [here].

Ninth: This refers to the "I" (ātman) in relation to the six [faculties] and the two [objects]. Thus, they constitute nine. Question: As for the "I" that follows separately from the six and the two, under which category is it subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed by neither. It is not like the latter two [categories], because all names exist [therein], and thus it is not pervasive (*sāmānya*).

Nor is it like the former six, because it receives its name through a specific meaning (*viśeṣa*). Furthermore, since it is not subsumed by either the single or the combined categories below, the agent (*kartṛ*) is added along with the instigator (*prayojaka*).
The term "name" (*nāman*) is itself called "heavy" (*guru*), because it refers repeatedly to the agent. As for that which is based upon this practice: it is based upon the very faculties;
that which is practiced is the object traversed by consciousness, because it is produced from the substance of the six consciousnesses.

Because it possesses the sense of "producing" and explains the meaning of the "bases" (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) of consciousness neither increase nor decrease; that is to say, they do not decrease within the middle, nor do they increase within the middle. Thus they are established.

Huijue says: "The two kinds [of grasping] are based upon the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature). They are based on the characteristics (*nimitta*) and the views (*darśana*) of self and dharmas;

these characteristics and views are themselves forms of grasping. Furthermore, regarding the separate interpretation that follows [the previous one], both are the interpretations of the Shuyou (樞要) school.

The phrase 'those characteristics all depend on what is transformed by consciousness'—as for the mention of 'same' and 'different,' there is a correspondence and a distinction with the subsequent passage stating 'transformation refers to the substance of consciousness.'"
Therefore, this [interpretation] is precisely the meaning of Dharmapāla’s defense; Sthiramati does not accept it.

Because the grasping of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) relies upon the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), that which is called "the transformed" refers to the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Since these are what have been transformed by the self-cognizing portion, the two graspings of self and phenomena arise based upon that which has been transformed.

"Because the three factors are of the same kind" refers to the view that when one perceives a reflected image and its original object, this is a divergent interpretation from the West; it does not mention the name of the master [who held it]. Its intent is to clarify that all things are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and that there are no external objects apart from the mind; thus, it states that the three factors arise as a single kind within the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). As for the phrase "the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the seeing-part, and the original object are the same because their seeds, both new and old, are identical": [This means that] the seeds of the image-aspect, the seeing-part, and the original object are identical, whether they be newly produced or previously existing. Therefore, these three factors arise together as a single kind. This is the meaning. The informative [act] (*vijñapti*) is neither received from another nor received by oneself; rather, it is simply the non-arising of transgressions. The volition (*cetanā*) that co-exists with the precepts is designated as "precept" (*śīla*) in its conventional sense.

Upon this actual manifestation, one establishes the "prātimokṣa" (individual liberation). This refers to what is received by the seven classes of followers, wherein each separately guards against wrongdoing.

This requires that the arising of the informative act gives rise to the non-informative (*avijñapti*). Since the single moment of the informative precept immediately passes away, all subsequent moments consist solely of the non-informative, which is the seed.

Standing above [the previous categories], because it is obtained by begging from others, one adds a vow (*praṇidhāna*). Likewise, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) arises through instruction and exhortation, such as requesting the Dharma from others;

thus, phenomena such as volition (*cetanā*) and vows give rise to what is called "bad morality" (*duḥśīla*), which is non-restraint. Regarding the intermediate non-manifest (*avijñapti*) and so forth:
because a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) cannot infuse seeds, that which is subtle within both the wholesome and unwholesome realms is termed "intermediate" (*madhyama*).

Because it is intermediate, it is simply called "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*). It is the action of a body that moves; when *cetanā* (volition) receives the name "action," it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative compound).

When the body receives the name "action," it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compound). Bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) depends upon the body and is itself the intimation; thus, it is strictly a *karmadhāraya*.

Regarding the meaning of non-intimation (*avijñapti*), among the three types of volition, it consists of the two meanings of deliberation (*santīraṇa*), determination (*niścaya*), and initiation (*prerana*); these produce the fruit.

Meaning (*artha*). The meaning of "wandering" (*yāna*): because initial volition (*cetanā*) is capable of producing a result and is not itself wandered upon by another, it is exclusively the single [volitional] meaning.

It is not that the King does not manifest himself, nor that the Victorious One (*jina*) does not manifest others. This meaning of victory (*vijaya*) applies both to volition and to speech. The intended sense is that one causes others to accomplish evil or good;
thus, in every respect, it constitutes the meaning of "formative action" (*abhisamskāra*). If this is so, how can body and speech produce [results]? [They do so] by causing others to act.

The accomplishment of good, evil, and so forth, arises both from grasping (*upādāna*) and from one’s own volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*). These various constructions are merely instances of intentional volition (*cetanā*).

Because the general and the specific are governed by this sovereign factor, intentional volition is designated as "manifest" (*vijñapti*), while the realization of thought is established under the name of "action" (*karman*). Question:

second, because the Buddha does not sever the continuity of existence. Regarding the statement, "If it is produced in every moment, it is therefore named 'birth' (*jāti*) and so forth," this explains "birth" among the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).

It is named "birth" simply because it arises from another. First, [if birth were self-originated], there would be no fruit of itself. Second, it would not be established as a cause of itself. Thus, one should investigate.

Because it applies to both the inner and outer paths as well as the teachings of the three vehicles, those of no-nature (abhāva) raise two obstacles and ask specifically about them.

Because the body possesses the seeds of the three realms (*dhātu*), if these seeds were to manifest individually, then when one is in a lower realm but has attained a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a higher realm, the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of that higher realm would arise within the body, resulting in confusion.
Therefore, one must take only those [seeds] that belong to the same level (*bhūmi*) as the eighth consciousness; in this way, their substance is established.
